1.pericope_label: In Judah is God known: in Salem also is his tabernacle: there brake he the arrows of the bow

schools.summary: Augustine reports that the Jews glory in this psalm and revile the Gentiles to whom God is unknown, and turns the boast round by making Judah the inward circumcision of the heart, so that those who glory in the name while having lost the deeds are Jews in flesh and heathens in heart.

Gill refers the knowledge of God to those who are Jews inwardly and the true circumcision, and reads the tabernacle further of the human nature in which the Word dwelt; Calvin sets aside the deliverance from the Ammonites for the destruction of the Assyrian army, cites the Greek title naming the Assyrian, and holds the psalm later than David so that either an older singer’s work was adopted or a descendant of the same name wrote it.

Henry makes the knowledge of God the greater favour for being distinguishing, has God keeping court in Zion and issuing orders by his oracles, and remembers that a tabernacle is a movable dwelling so that the light is with us yet a little while; Spurgeon says that if God were unknown in all the world beside he is no unknown God to his people, and compresses the third verse into one sentence, that without leaving his tranquil abode he snapped his enemies’ arrows before they could shoot them.

Clarke collects three proposed occasions, the Syriac thanksgiving for the taking of a city of Ammon, the Latin and Greek psalm for the Assyrians, and the defeat of Sennacherib, holds the psalm later than David and the author a different singer of the same name, and identifies the arrows as the fiery kind with a Roman name, a line of Virgil and an old commentator’s description of the weapon; Wesley takes the battle for all the power of the army put in array.

Keil and Delitzsch hold that no psalm coincides so exactly with a known historical situation as this does with the overthrow of the Assyrian army, and take the mountains of prey for haughty possessors of power who plunder all who come near; Ellicott finds the four place-names arranged by introversion and chosen for the rhythm, proposes that the received renderings obliterate the image of a crouching beast of prey and would translate covert and lair, doubts the old identification of the patriarchs’ Salem with Jerusalem, and offers three derivations of the word for arrows without choosing.

debates: What occasion does the psalm celebrate? Keil and Delitzsch and Calvin both settle on the overthrow of the Assyrian army before Jerusalem and both cite the Greek title that names the Assyrian, Keil and Delitzsch adding that companion psalms in the same collection answer to a later deliverance by mutual massacre; Calvin reports that other deliverance as a proposal for this psalm and sets it aside; Clarke adds a third possibility from the Syriac, a thanksgiving for the taking of a city of the children of Ammon.

What does it mean that God is known in Judah? Augustine reports the Jewish boast and converts it, making the true Judah the circumcision of the heart, so that those who keep the name and lose the deeds are heathens in heart; Gill takes the same turn; Henry keeps the sense national and makes the knowledge a distinguishing favour; Spurgeon makes it the church’s privilege against a dark outer world; Clarke says simply that the true God revealed himself to the Jews.

Is the second verse about a dwelling or a lair? Ellicott holds that the received renderings quite obliterate the image, which is a beast of prey crouching ready to spring, and translates covert and lair; Gill, Clarke, Henry and Wesley all keep the tabernacle and the dwelling place, Henry adding that a tabernacle is movable; Keil and Delitzsch, without touching the second verse, keep the predatory register at the mountains of prey.
outliers: Clarke identifies the arrows as incendiary, with inflammable matter rolled round the heads and ignited, shot into towns to fire them and among the wooden works of besiegers, gives their Roman name, quotes a line of Virgil, and reports an old commentator describing the weapon as a dart with a spherical leaden head, named from the towers it was thrown from.

Ellicott offers three derivations of the word for arrows without choosing between them: the lightning speed of an arrow in flight, the custom of shooting bolts tipped with flame, or a connection with a word that elsewhere denotes pestilence.

Ellicott finds the four place-names of the opening arranged by introversion, the restricted terms standing first and last and the general ones in the middle, and holds the order chosen simply for the rhythm.

Calvin and Clarke independently conclude that the psalm is later than David and that its author cannot be the singer of David’s day, but either a descendant of the same name or an older writer whose work was adopted for the occasion.
themes: a boast turned inside out
a dwelling read as a lair
arrows that carry fire
a psalm dated by the kingdoms it names
battle used to sum up all weapons

4.pericope_label: Thou art more glorious and excellent than the mountains of prey: the stouthearted are spoiled

schools.summary: Gill rejects the reading that addresses the fourth verse to Zion and refers it to God or Christ on the authority of an old paraphrase, offers an alternative rendering that makes the stout-hearted spoil themselves, and reads the verse a second time of principalities spoiled at the cross, of the strong man disarmed in conversion, and of the destruction of antichrist.

Clarke addresses the fourth verse to the mountain where God dwelt and contrasts it with mountains where wild beasts prey on the helpless, takes the destroying angel for a suffocating wind that killed men and horses alike in their tents in one night, and asks whether the line about the men of might is not a strong irony; Wesley refers the verse to God and explains the mountains as kings and empires established by tyranny and maintained by preying on their own subjects.

Ellicott abandons the comparative of the received English and renders that God is splendid, coming from the mountains of prey, notes an emendation making the word fearful rather than glorious, presses the mountains as those of the Lion of Judah before a new image interrupts with the hero shining in his spoils, renders the spoiling reflexively and the sleep as a sinking into deep slumber, writes a long note on finding one’s hands as an idiom of powerlessness, and traces the word for the sleep to a captain in the book of Judges and thence to two old victory songs; Keil and Delitzsch have God send his judiciary word from heaven into the din of war so that it was immediately silenced.

debates: Who or what is called more glorious than the mountains of prey? Gill reports that some take it of Zion and rejects that for God or Christ, citing an old paraphrase; Clarke takes precisely the reading Gill rejects and addresses the verse to the mountain where God dwelt; Wesley agrees with Gill on the addressee and makes the mountains kings and empires established by tyranny; Ellicott abandons the comparative altogether and renders that God is splendid, coming from the mountains of prey, which he takes for the hunting ground of the Lion of Judah.
outliers: Ellicott writes his longest note on the phrase about not finding one’s hands, observing that it grew naturally into an idiom in a language that used hand for strength, and quoting a Talmudic phrase about not finding one’s hands and feet in the school house from another commentator represented in this same collection, together with the Virgilian use of the word for hands and a phrase of Shakespeare about a proper fellow of my hands.

Ellicott traces the word for the deep sleep to the slumber of a defeated captain in the book of Judges, holds that two old victory songs were in the poet’s mind, and notes that the same songs have since inspired the well-known lines of Byron on Sennacherib.
Clarke naturalises the destroying angel as a suffocating wind, which killed the sleeping camp and its horses alike in a single night.

Ellicott renders the spoiling reflexively, that the stout-hearted have let themselves be spoiled, the picture being of men rendered powerless at a glance and a word; Gill independently reports an alternative that makes them spoil themselves.
themes: a comparative abandoned
mountains read as empires and as hunting grounds
an idiom for powerlessness traced through three languages
an angel explained as a wind
a psalm that reaches a Romantic poem

7.pericope_label: Thou, even thou, art to be feared: thou didst cause judgment to be heard from heaven; the earth feared, and was still

schools.summary: Henry states the supposition of thunder and earthquake in full and then refuses it as altogether uncertain, takes the event as a lesson to the whole world, compares the silence of the earth to the silence made by proclamation when a court sits, asks who may stand in God’s sight from the minute he is angry and answers with chaff and stubble before a consuming fire, and defines the meek as those who can bear any wrong but do none, for whom God will sooner or later plead.

Gill reports the supposition of a violent clap of thunder as the voice of God at the destruction of the army, notes on an interpreter’s authority that all decrees come from heaven, and extends the judgment forward to the vials of wrath decreed against the antichristian states and then to the last judgment, with the archangel’s voice, the last trumpet and the dead rising to hear sentence.

Clarke moves the hearing back to the prophet’s declaration that the enemy should not prevail, takes the earth that feared for the land and by metonymy its inhabitants, struck motionless with terror, and makes the meek the humbled and oppressed people of the land, the poor Jews now utterly helpless; Wesley allows either thunders and earthquakes or the quick spread of the report as the reason the judgment is said to be heard.

Ellicott restricts the meek to the land rather than the earth in a gloss of four words; Keil and Delitzsch pass over the scene quickly and treat the following verse about the wrath of man as the general truth of which this deliverance is a single instance.

debates: How was the judgment heard from heaven? Gill reports that some think there was a violent clap of thunder, thunder being the voice of God; Wesley allows that or the quick spreading abroad of the report; Henry states the thunder and the earthquake as the supposition of those who date the psalm from the Assyrian defeat and dismisses it as altogether uncertain; Clarke moves the hearing back to the prophet’s declaration beforehand, so that what was heard was a prophecy and not a noise.

Is it the earth or the land that feared? Clarke takes it for the land and by metonymy its inhabitants, and makes the meek the oppressed people of that land; Ellicott glosses the same word as of the land rather than of the earth; Henry takes the event as a lesson to all the world.
outliers: Henry compares the stillness of the earth to the silence made by proclamation when a court sits.
Henry defines the meek as those who can bear any wrong but do none, and holds that God takes what is done against them as done against himself.

Gill carries the judgment heard from heaven forward from the Assyrian army to the vials of wrath decreed against the antichristian states and then to the last judgment itself, with the archangel’s voice, the last trumpet, and the dead rising to hear sentence pronounced.
Clarke locates the hearing of the judgment not in any sound at the time but in the prophet’s earlier declaration that the enemy should not prevail.
themes: thunder proposed and declined
the earth shrunk to a land
silence made as at the opening of a court
meekness defined by what it will not do
one deliverance read as an instance of a rule

10.pericope_label: Surely the wrath of man shall praise thee: vow, and pay unto the Lord your God: he shall cut off the spirit of princes

schools.summary: Gill allows the wrath of the tenth verse to be God’s own with man for its object, denies that the vows meant are monastic or ceremonial and makes them the spiritual sacrifices of praise that men vow in distress and ought to pay when delivered, and offers three senses of what is cut off from princes, their pride, their courage or their life, the word signifying the cutting of a bunch of grapes.

Clarke keeps the received text of the tenth verse and reads God girding himself with wrath as a man girds himself to work, reports the very different Latin about the thought of man and the remains of thought keeping a feast, draws the maxim that God does not permit men to go the full length of what they purposed, takes the second half of the eleventh verse of the neighbouring nations bringing homage to the terrible One, and turns the last verse into an indictment of conquerors who laid countries waste and made widows and orphans without number; Wesley makes the praise come from the spectators and the cutting off a vintage.

Ellicott declares the received text of the tenth verse unintelligible, takes an emendation from the Greek and the Latin by which the residue of wraths does God honour, identifies that residue with those who escape the enemy’s rage, compares a phrase of Virgil for the remnants of a defeated host, and suggests a rendering that carries the thought back to the escape from Egypt and the festival demanded of Pharaoh; he also divides the eleventh verse between Israelites and heathen. Keil and Delitzsch print the closing verses without comment.

debates: Is the second clause of the tenth verse sound? Ellicott calls the received text unintelligible and emends it from the Greek and the Latin so that the residue of wraths does God honour, the residue being those who escape the enemy’s rage; Clarke keeps the text and reads God girding himself with the remainder of wrath as a man girds himself to work, while reporting a Latin reading about the thought of man that differs from both; Gill and Wesley keep the received sense without raising the question.

Whom does the call to vow and pay address? Ellicott divides the verse, the first clause going to the Israelites and the second to the heathen; Clarke reads the second half of the neighbouring nations who bring homage to the terrible One lest they be consumed as the Assyrians were; Wesley has all the neighbouring nations submit; Gill takes the whole as addressed to those delivered from wrath.
outliers: Ellicott compares the residue of wrath to a phrase of Virgil for the remnants of a defeated host, the second citation of that poet in this chapter, Clarke having quoted him on the fiery arrows.
Clarke reports the Latin reading of the tenth verse, that the thought of man shall praise God and the remains of thought keep a feast day to him, and marks how different it is from the Hebrew.

Gill denies that the vows of the eleventh verse are monastic, saying the Papists would infer as much from such words, and makes them the spiritual sacrifices of praise vowed in distress and paid on deliverance.

Clarke turns the last verse into an indictment of conquerors who from the lust of dominion laid countries waste by fire and sword, making widows and orphans without number, and holds that judging those whom man cannot bring to justice is one grand use of a final judgment day.
themes: a verse called unintelligible and mended
wrath worn as a working girdle
survivors read as the residue
princes cut like grapes
a court for those no court can reach
